theorems: Order of an element modulo p
problems.notes: The core idea is to show that if m>1, any prime divisor p of m also divides 2^(2^m)+1, leading to a contradiction regarding the order of 2 modulo p. This forces m=1, reducing the problem to finding n such that n divides 5(2^(2n)+1). Uses properties of gcd(n, 2^(2n)+1).

A problem about the maximum possible number of students (n) in a test scenario where answers are limited, ensuring a specific condition on identical answers. Requires combinatorial reasoning and application of the pigeonhole principle.

The solution cleverly defines R as the left-hand side and applies a chain of inequalities comparing R to weighted arithmetic means. It's a specific case (n=4) of a more general inequality valid for any n positive numbers.

The problem asks for the existence of a number below 10^9 representable in over 1000 ways as a sum of three distinct natural squares. The solution counts the number of representations for numbers up to N and finds an N (18003) where the average representation count exceeds 1000, implying existence.

A complex geometry problem requiring the construction of a line parallel to AB through D, introducing points Q and K, and extensive angle chasing to show two sets of four points are concyclic, ultimately proving A, P, M, N are concyclic.

A tiling/coloring problem. The solution describes a coloring strategy for an n x n square divided into unit squares. It uses an averaging argument on the number of colored unit squares a larger x x x square can cover, proving that for large enough n, any such square must contain unit squares of at least 4 different colors.
